title: Data frames
text:
A data frame is a rectangular collection of vectors of equal length. Each column is a vector (a variable). Each row is an observation. Different columns can contain different types of data.

# create one
travellers <- data.frame(
  name = c("Arthur", "Ford", "Trillian", "Zaphod"),
  planet = c("Earth", "Betelgeuse", "Earth", "Betelgeuse"),
  age = c(30, 200, 30, NA),
  towels = c(1, 2, 1, 0), 
  knows_answer = c(NA, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))




travellers

      name     planet age towels knows_answer
1   Arthur      Earth  30      1           NA
2     Ford Betelgeuse 200      2         TRUE
3 Trillian      Earth  30      1         TRUE
4   Zaphod Betelgeuse  NA      0        FALSE

# look at the top rows
head(travellers, 2)

    name     planet age towels knows_answer
1 Arthur      Earth  30      1           NA
2   Ford Betelgeuse 200      2         TRUE

# look at the bottom rows
tail(travellers, 2)

      name     planet age towels knows_answer
3 Trillian      Earth  30      1         TRUE
4   Zaphod Betelgeuse  NA      0        FALSE

names(travellers)

[1] "name"         "planet"       "age"          "towels"       "knows_answer"






class(travellers$name) 

[1] "character"

class(travellers$age) 

[1] "numeric"

nrow(travellers)

[1] 4

ncol(travellers)

[1] 5

length(travellers$name) 

[1] 4

length(travellers$age)

[1] 4

dim(travellers)

[1] 4 5

Note



When you read or save a file, R needs to know where to look for it. The folder R is currently using is called the working directory.
You can check it with:

getwd()

[1] "/Users/nleach/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-TUEindhoven/Teaching/another-intro-r"


Rather than repeatedly changing the working directory with setwd(), it is better to work inside an RStudio project and use relative file paths.
Tip: Session > Set Working Directory > To File Source Location

title: R as a calculator
text:
3 + 1 - 2

[1] 2

(3 * 4) / 2

[1] 6

3^2

[1] 9

# Division 
15 / 6

[1] 2.5

15 %/% 6 # integer part

[1] 2

15 %% 6 # remainder

[1] 3









x <- 3 
y = 3 





y == x 

[1] TRUE

x == 6

[1] FALSE

y != x 

[1] FALSE






(x < 5) & (y == 5)

[1] FALSE

(x < 5) | (y == 5)

[1] TRUE








vectors
data frames (and tibbles)
matrices (and arrays)
lists





one-dimensional collection of values

Common vector types/classes:

logical: TRUE / FALSE
numeric: a vector that contains numbers
character: a vector that contains strings of text


logical_vector   <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
numeric_vector   <- c(4, 5.2, pi)
character_vector <- c("four", "five", "six")

More info see: r-bloggers

# c() creates a vector
1v <- c(4, "four", 1+pi)

# [ ] lets you subset from the vector 
v[3]


1

Atomic vectors can only contain one type. So adding a character to your vector makes all the values characters (coercion)




[1] "4.14159265358979"








Note




v_character <- c("four", 1+pi, 1.5+exp(1), 'almost four')# "" vs '' is preference
is.character(v_character)

[1] TRUE

class(v_character) 

[1] "character"

typeof(v_character) 

[1] "character"



v_numeric <- c(4, 1+pi, 1.5+exp(1))
is.numeric(v_numeric)

[1] TRUE

class(v_numeric) # high-level data structure - user's perspective

[1] "numeric"

typeof(v_numeric) # internal representation

[1] "double"


returns “double” because by default numeric values are stored as “double-precision numbers”

title: Getting started
text:
Installing R
R is a programming language for statistical computing and data analysis, while RStudio provides a user-friendly interface for working with R.

install R from R Project website
install RStudio

There are plenty of tutorials (e.g: QLS-MiCM)

title: Getting started
text:
Actually starting
After installing both R and RStudio, open RStudio, in the Console type:

print("Hello world")
3 + 2
?mean

Make a new file:

In the menu File > New File > Rscript
Type 40 + 2 in the newly created script, then click Ctrl+Enter
Alternatively: select 40 + 2 and click on ‘Run’
To save the R script: File > Save / Save as.
